content: Studies have frequently reported various challenges associated with HIV testing services. These include issues such as difficulties in specimen collection, incorrect execution of test procedures, reading test results outside the recommended time frame, and misinterpretation of test results. Inadequate supervision and poor management of testing kits have led to stock-outs and the use of damaged or expired rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs). In some instances, testing was conducted by inadequately trained staff who lacked sufficient understanding of testing during the window period, retesting after discrepant results, or verifying HIV diagnoses prior to initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART). Few testing sites participated in external quality assessment (EQA) schemes, and poor record-keeping, data collection, and transcription errors were noted. One study found that nearly 30% of errors resulted in incorrect test results. Some studies also highlighted challenges in interpreting weak reactive test lines, which were sometimes misinterpreted as negative results. The implementation of quality management systems (QMS) is essential for all forms of HIV testing services (HTS), whether conducted in laboratories, health facilities, community settings, or through self-testing. QMS is necessary regardless of the type of assay used, such as RDTs or immunoassays, and regardless of who conducts the testing, including trained laboratory personnel, healthcare professionals, lay providers, or self-testers. QMS encompasses all organizational processes required to ensure quality, including quality assurance (QA), quality control (QC), and quality improvement (QI). Quality assurance focuses on providing confidence that quality requirements will be met by preventing errors and defects in products and services. It is proactive in nature. Quality control, on the other hand, verifies that the product meets quality requirements and identifies defects, formally rejecting defective products. QC is more reactive and focuses on the quality of the actual product being used. Quality improvement involves proposing solutions to enhance quality and reliability, thereby increasing customer satisfaction. The plan–do–check–act cycle is a useful tool for QI. WHO guidance on QI is available in the policy brief Maintaining and improving quality of care within HIV clinical services. Quality management emphasizes the quality of processes required for effective testing, of which the quality of the product (the in vitro diagnostic device, or IVD) is only one aspect. Engaging with all individuals involved in the testing process is critical, including staff responsible for procurement, those establishing and supervising health facilities, testing providers (including self-test distributors), and clients. Record-keeping and documentation also play a significant role in ensuring the quality of testing and are integral to QMS. A testing service that uses high-quality products but suffers from stock-outs, improper use of test kits, or inconvenient operating hours cannot be considered a high-quality service. Everyone involved in testing services shares responsibility for maintaining quality. The quality of HTS is suboptimal in many settings, but simple measures can significantly improve quality. WHO guidelines on differentiated HIV testing services provide detailed recommendations for improving HTS quality, particularly in resource-limited settings where RDTs and other IVDs are commonly used, and staff often have multiple responsibilities beyond testing. For more information on self-testing quality management, refer to the WHO self-testing framework. At the national level, certain aspects of a QMS must be addressed, including national policies, strategic plans, and monitoring processes to support QMS at testing sites. Workforce development is critical, ensuring that testing providers are adequately trained and supervised. Regulation of IVDs, including the use of WHO’s prequalification listing to identify quality IVDs, reporting user feedback, and strengthening regulatory capacities, is essential. Testing strategies and algorithms should align with WHO recommendations, and procurement and supply chain management must ensure uninterrupted supply and proper storage of test kits. Accreditation of testing sites is also necessary to uphold quality standards. National policies for HIV testing should be regularly updated and linked to other national policies and strategic plans, such as those for laboratory operations and health and human resources. National authorities, often through the national reference laboratory or the ministry of health, are responsible for planning, implementing, and monitoring quality activities for HIV testing. These activities may include on-site supportive supervision visits, certification of testing sites, provision of third-party quality-control materials (proficiency testing), and follow-up on corrective actions arising from quality activities. Proficiency testing (PT) for HIV diagnostic tests, as well as other laboratory tests used to monitor treatment, is a priority to ensure the accuracy and reliability of test results. Providers of proficiency panels should be accredited according to ISO standards (ISO 17043) or actively pursuing ISO accreditation. ISO accreditation assures the provider’s competence in planning and implementing PT programs. Workforce development is essential for ensuring quality testing. This includes standardized and coordinated pre-service and in-service training with hands-on practicums and competency-based assessments. National policies should support task-sharing, allowing lay providers to conduct testing and issue HIV diagnosis reports. Recruitment and retention strategies should prioritize rural and underserved areas. Certification of testing providers can serve as an incentive to reinforce the quality of HIV testing activities. Digital health tools have been leveraged to improve HIV testing quality. For example, South Africa’s Rapid Test Continuous Quality Improvement (RTCQI) initiative, supported by WHO and the CDC, has transitioned from paper-based tools to a digital platform. This platform includes mobile apps for data collection, real-time dashboards for data review, and e-learning modules for training. The digital approach has facilitated timely identification of quality issues and targeted interventions, significantly improving facility ratings and tester competency. Regulation of IVDs directly impacts the quality of HIV testing. WHO’s global model regulatory framework for medical devices, including IVDs, provides guiding principles and harmonized definitions for effective regulation. WHO prequalification assesses whether IVDs meet the highest standards of quality, safety, and performance. This process includes dossier review, QMS inspection, and independent evaluation of performance and operational characteristics. Post-market surveillance is also critical, requiring manufacturers to monitor product performance and address any quality, safety, or performance issues. Collaborative registration procedures, such as reliance on WHO prequalification outcomes, can streamline national regulatory processes while maintaining regulatory autonomy. This approach saves resources and ensures high-quality regulatory decisions. Post-market surveillance further ensures that products continue to meet quality standards after being placed on the market.
